summary: With Allow typos on, a name search that nothing matches with its letters in order lists only near misses, where it listed everything fff-search's own typo matching returned. In `Engine::search` the fallback keeps a hit only if each checked word is an in-order subsequence of `hit.rel` or `near_miss(word, rel, typo_budget(word))`: Sellers' approximate substring match with the adjacent-swap case (optimal string alignment), with 0 typos for a word of up to 3 letters, 1 for 4 to 7, 2 for 8 or more, counted in chars. `rel` is the path inside the folder searched, so a folder search for a word in the folder's own name no longer lists the whole folder. `checked_words(&words)` leaves out words shorter than two bytes when the search has a longer one, as fff-search does (`valid_parts`); the strict check, the fallback, `app_hits` (review) and `strict_words`, which `changes_for` goes by, all use it, while `rerank`, the sort helpers, `wants_apps` and the highlight needle keep every word. Review added `may_be_spelled_apart(word, rel)`: where the word and the path both have a letter beyond ASCII, fff-search's match stands. Files: crates/fffinder-core/src/engine.rs, docs/manual.md (the unquoted-words paragraph, Ranking and limits, the Allow typos row, the settings.json `typos` row).
changelog: With **Allow typos** on, a name search that nothing matches without typos now lists only near misses. It used to list everything fff-search's own typo matching returned, which lets a word go without two of its letters or more and takes the rest from anywhere along the path, so `bduget` listed `debug-test.log` beside `budget.txt`, and `xqz` listed every name with an x, a q, or a z. A near miss has the word in one place with one typo: a letter that is wrong, missing, or one too many, or two letters side by side that have changed places. A word of eight letters or more can have two typos, and a word of three letters or fewer none. Searching one folder for a word that is in the folder's own name no longer lists everything in the folder. Some searches that found their item among those results now find nothing: a typo together with gaps (`prjatlz` for `Project Atlas.txt`), two typos in a word shorter than eight letters, and a typo in a word of three letters or fewer. A word with an accent or in another alphabet is held to this only where a path is all in A to Z, digits, and symbols: a name can store a letter such as `ñ` as one character or as two, as macOS does, so other paths are still listed for such a word as loosely as before. A single letter from A to Z, digit, or symbol beside a longer word no longer narrows a search to the paths that have it somewhere: `a budget` finds every budget, and `photo 2` finds every photo, with `photo 2.jpg` ahead of the others. `fff find` follows the same rules.
behaviour_changes: Everything here goes for name searches wherever Engine::search is used: the window, Smart Folders, the file chooser, `fff find`.

Allow typos on, and nothing has every checked word's letters in order: only near misses are listed. Demo folder, the window's search, my own before and after: `bduget` 5 -> 1 (Budget.csv), `raodmap` 4 -> 2, `idnex` 131 -> 1, `noets` 156 -> 3, `reprot q1` 31 -> 1, `tniy` 144 -> 1, `darft` 129 -> 1, `xqz` 132 -> 0, `teh` 164 -> 0, `biult` 124 -> 0. In the 42,275 files of the cargo registry: `thisdoesnotexist`, `zxcvbnm`, `levenshtein` 500 -> 0, `smtih waterman` 500 -> 21 (the files under smith_waterman/).

Searches that found their item among those results and now find nothing: a typo together with gaps (`prjatlz` 6 -> 0), two typos in a word under eight letters (`bugdte` 4 -> 0), any typo in a word of three letters or fewer (`lbi` 146 -> 0, where lib.rs was the seventh row).

A folder search for a word that is only in the folder's own name: No Results in place of the whole folder (`research` in Research 5 -> 0, `many` in Many 120 -> 0, `2026` in Tax [2026] 2 -> 0). With empty-state-messages on the trunk the message reads "The search looked only in “Research”." with a Search This Computer button (picture review-after-folder-research).

A single ASCII letter, digit or symbol beside a longer word is not looked for, with Allow typos on and off: `a budget` lists every budget, `photo 1` and `photo 2` each list both demo photos (1 -> 2), the named one first. In my home-like fixture `invoce 7` 15 -> 165 and `report 2` 220 -> 500 with a `+`: all 148 reports with a 2 in their names are still listed, the first 36 rows have one, after that names with and without mix. Such a search lists what the longer words alone list (28 pairs such as `q atlas` and `atlas`, in four kinds of search with Allow typos on and off: 208 comparisons, the same items in each pair wherever the limit didn't cut the list), apps included (review).

Apps (review): an app is found by the same words, so `a budget` finds an app named Budget and `photo 2` finds Photos; before the review an app still had to have the lone letter in its name. A lone letter no longer adds to an app's score either, as it adds nothing to a file's; rerank's name bonuses still count it.

A word with a letter beyond ASCII (review): on a path that has such a letter too, the hit is kept as fff-search matched it, as before this change; on a path all in ASCII the near-miss rule holds. In a fixture of 22 files whose accents are stored apart, 21 searches typed with composed letters (`señor`, `résumé`, `crème brûlée`, `münchen` …): the trunk listed the file in all 21, first or second; the implementer's commit in 3; the commit on the trunk in all 21, among the first four rows, without the ASCII-named far misses (`señor` 7 -> 5 rows, `crème` 22 -> 18).

Searches whose words are all single letters, or one letter beside only filters, are checked as before, but their fallback is the near-miss rule, which a letter cannot pass: `q *.csv` with no q in any csv path lists nothing (was every csv), and `d q`, which fff-search answers with every folder, lists nothing (demo, the window's search: 12 folders -> 0).
Live results: `changes_for` goes by the checked words, so a search with a lone letter runs again for a new file that has the other words (`k tax` and a new Tax Return.pdf).

Unchanged: a search with a result that has every checked word in order lists what it listed (the same rows, scores and order unless a lone letter was typed), everything with Allow typos off except the lone-letter rule, contents searches, `fff files`, `total_matched`.

Cost, in the fallback only, debug build, one search thread, the 42,275-file tree: the slowest fallback search took 74 to 93 ms (`thisdoesnotexist`), against 50 to 70 ms for the slowest searches outside the fallback; with a limit of 5,000, which fetches 20,000 candidates, 217 ms against 250 ms for `serde`. Demo folder: under 12 ms.
left_out: The optional UI test in tests/controls.rs: the window, `fff find`, Smart Folders and the chooser all go through Engine::search, which the engine tests cover, and the pictures are of the real window.
The optional doc comment on SearchSettings::typos in config.rs, which is still true.
A folder name typed alone (`src/`) and a word with a line suffix alone (`main.rs:42`) give the check no words, so they still list everything fff-search returns, with Allow typos on or off.
Ranking and highlights, as the verifier planned: near-miss rows have no highlight and are not ranked by how close they are; a row that lacks a lone letter of the search has no highlight either.
Thresholds are the proposal's (3/7/8), not the verifier's stricter option.
`changes_for` still passes over a new file that is only a near miss, as the manual says: it waits for Refresh.
Normalizing names and words (NFC), which would make the review's exemption unnecessary: it needs a crate (see notes).
CHANGELOG.md, per the guide; the entry is the commit's Changelog paragraph.
`cargo clippy --features term`: nothing under src/term uses what changed, and every changed function is private to engine.rs.

review_fixes: crates/fffinder-core/src/engine.rs, `may_be_spelled_apart` in the fallback: the implementer's filter made a search for a file by its own name find nothing where the name stores an accent apart from its letter, which is how macOS's Finder and most Mac apps write names, while a keyboard types the one character. Letter for letter `señor.txt` is then two typos from `señor`. On the trunk such names are found only through fff-search's loose matching, in the fallback. Now a word with a letter beyond ASCII keeps fff-search's match on a path that has such a letter too. New test, with each half of the condition pinned by a mutation.

crates/fffinder-core/src/engine.rs, `app_hits` is given the checked words: `a budget` listed Budget.csv and not an app named Budget, and the manual's sentence that a lone letter isn't looked for was false for apps. `checked_words` returns owned words for it, which also shortens `strict_words`. Two assertions in finds_apps_without_indexing_them.

docs/manual.md: `photo 2` finds everything that `photo` finds (apps too); the Allow typos row says where a word with an accent or in another alphabet is held to the rule, and its last sentence no longer leans on the one before it.
Commit message: a paragraph for the spelling exemption, apps in the lone-letter paragraph, one sentence more in the Changelog paragraph.

Rebase onto ca4fbee, d85ca95 (result-tie-break) and f60d2e4 (empty-state-messages): one conflict, in the manual's Ranking and limits paragraph, resolved to keep result-tie-break's three new sentences and this change's typo sentences. engine.rs merged by itself: the check sits where it did, before `rerank` and `raw.sort_by(by_rank)`.
Nothing else was changed. I found no fault in near_miss, typo_budget, checked_words or the strict_words change (see notes).
notes:
Checked. check.sh printed CHECK OK on the trunk commit 5624239 after the rebase: 692 passed in 16 test binaries, 3 of 3 known root-only failures (662 before the rebase, 661 on the implementer's commit). `git push . HEAD:search-ui-polish` fast-forwarded f60d2e4..5624239.

I did not go around it. `git ls-remote origin` reads f60d2e4 for search-ui-polish; the commit is on the local trunk and the next integration carries it.

How it was checked. (1) The tests against the trunk's check: with the two behaviour hunks reverse-applied and the helpers kept, 4 of the implementer's 7 tests fail (a_typo_finds_only_near_misses, a_lone_letter_beside_longer_words_isnt_looked_for, and the two changes_for tests), the two pure ones pass because the helpers are there, and quoted_words_match_names_letter_for_letter is a pin that passes either way. Applied again, the lane was clean. (2) near_miss against a reference of my own (optimal string alignment by the book between the word and every run of letters of the text) in a temporary test: 120,000 random pairs over four alphabets, one with é, ж and 日, at budgets 0 to 4: 600,000 comparisons, all equal, 336,006 of them near misses. (3) A model of the check written apart from it (which words are held, strict or fallback, the budgets) inside a temporary probe that reads the hits as they are before the check: 11,976 searches on the rebased code with no mismatch (the demo folder; a home-like fixture of 3,065 files in two search locations with an app folder; 22 names with accents stored apart; the 42,275 files of the cargo registry), each with Allow typos on and off, in the window's kind of search, files only, Folder, Document and Image, and in ten folders. The same probe run against the trunk's check matched a model of the old rule, also with no mismatch. (4) Old against new search by search, for the numbers under behaviour_changes. (5) Five pictures of my own, light and dark. All temporary code is gone from the lane.

The three ways I thought this most likely to hurt a user, and what I found. (1) A search that found its item now finds nothing. For names in ASCII that happens only where the rule says so (gaps with a typo, two typos under eight letters, a typo in three letters or fewer). For names that store accents apart it happened for almost every typed accent: that is the first review fix. (2) The lone-letter rule lists things the user did not ask for, or lists files and apps by different rules. It lists what the longer words list, ranked by the letter; apps did go by another rule, which is the second review fix. A digit used to narrow (`photo 2`), and now only ranks: the orchestrator's note asks for exactly this, the manual says it, and I kept it. (3) The fallback is slow on a large tree. It is not: see Cost.

For the briefs still to come:
- multi-word-highlights: `checked_words(&words)` (now `Vec<String>`, computed right after `words` in Engine::search) is what a result is held to; the highlight needle is still every word, so a row that lacks a lone letter of the search has no highlight at all (photo 1.jpg for `photo 2`, picture review-after-photo-2), and neither has a near-miss row or a row kept by `may_be_spelled_apart`, whose name does not have the word as typed. Highlight by the checked words first, and the lone letters where a name has them.
- query-history-boost: `app_hits` takes `&checked`, not `&words`; `wants_apps`, `rerank`, `sort_can_choose` and `cut_in_order` still take `words`. The fallback filter is the `else` branch of the strict check and runs before `rerank`.
- search-settings-hints-steppers: a hint for Allow typos should say what the manual's row says now: near misses, one typo (two from eight letters, none up to three), and that it is off for nothing else. The dialog's first row of Search Syntax ("typos allowed") still holds.
- search-start-no-flash, recent-searches: typo searches end in No Results more often.
- adhoc-index-feedback: in my probe the first 36 searches of a folder outside the search locations came back empty while its temporary index was built; nothing says so in the answer.

Found, not fixed (all on the trunk before this change unless said):
- The fallback is reached only when nothing has the letters in order anywhere along its path, and in a tree of any size something usually has, by accident. Then the real near miss is dropped as a typo match and the accidental matches are listed. In the cargo registry (42,275 files) all 27 misspellings of real names I tried (`carog`, `raedme`, `licnese`, `benchmrak`, `mainfest` …) listed such matches and never reached the fallback; `benchmrak` lists two normalizer benches and no benchmark.rs. In the home-like fixture (3,065 files, long names) 123 of 169 one-typo searches for words of the tree did not reach it, and for 31 of them nothing with the intended word was listed. So in large folders this change mostly turns the junk for words that match nothing into No Results; misspellings are helped only where no path has the letters in order. Worth a brief of its own: list near misses beside, or ahead of, matches whose letters are only scattered along the path when no name has the word in a row (`changes_for` would have to follow). One consequence that is new: a misspelled word beside a lone digit (`chpater 3`) used to reach the fallback because no accidental match had the digit, and listed chapter 3.mp4 first; now it lists what `chpater` alone lists.
- Names are compared as stored. A name whose accents are stored apart (macOS) never has a typed `é` in order, so such names are found only through the typo fallback, which the review's exemption keeps as it was: with fff-search's far misses among names that have such letters, without highlight, and not at all with Allow typos off or in a quoted word; an app with such a name is not found. A typo in a word typed without accents costs one typo more for every accent mark inside the run it is compared with (`bjrok` against a Björk stored apart), so it finds nothing where the old fallback listed the file. Normalizing names and words to one form (NFC) where `rel`, the app names and the words are made would fix all of it and make `may_be_spelled_apart` unnecessary; it needs the `unicode-normalization` crate, which is not in Cargo.lock (`icu_normalizer` is, through other crates). The other way round, a word typed without accents against a name that has them as one character is a wrong letter for each: `senor` finds `señor.txt`, `resume` does not find `Résumé.pdf` (two in six letters).
- Near misses are not ranked by where they are or how close: `mian` in the demo lists the 120 files of Many (their folder has `man`) ahead of main.rs, which is row 121 of 122 (124 of 142 before). A near miss in the name ahead of one in a folder's name would put it first.
- Apps are found by letters in order only, so `safair` does not find Safari.
- A folder name typed alone and a word with a line suffix alone are matched loosely and never checked (see left_out).
- CHANGELOG.md, for when it is assembled: the [Unreleased] entry on quoted words says unquoted words "match fuzzily across the whole path, so `taxexemptionc` can find a file whose folders spell it out between them". Corrected: "Unquoted words still match fuzzily along the path inside the search location, or inside the folder when only one is searched, so `taxexemptionc` also finds `tax/exemption/coding/Handler.java`, whose folders spell it out in order."

Doubts that remain.
1. macOS and Windows were not run. No platform-specific code was added. The new test writes two names with combining accents; APFS and NTFS keep a name as it is given, by what I know of them and not by a run, and the test accepts the name in either spelling back from the disk. That macOS stores accents apart for names made in Finder and Mac apps, and that typed text has them composed, is also from knowledge; the exemption does no harm where it is not so.
2. The exemption is wide: for a word with a letter beyond ASCII, every hit on a path with such a letter is kept as fff-search matched it. A Cyrillic, Greek or CJK word with a typo therefore still lists fff-search's far misses among names in those scripts (the implementer's version listed only near misses there, at the price above). Normalizing would let the rule cover them.
3. One typo in a word of four letters is loose, because the match is a run anywhere in the path: `mian` matches every `man`, `iocn` every `ion`. The thresholds are the brief's, and Algolia's defaults; the lists are far shorter than before, and the ranking item above is what would make them good.
4. A lone digit no longer narrows (`photo 2`, `chapter 3`). If it should, it is one condition in `checked_words` plus the manual sentence.
